newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli cabinet meets to set West Bank pullback.
newsitem.headline: Israeli cabinet meets to set West Bank pullback.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu convened Israel's cabinet on Thursday to set the scope of another handover of West Bank land to Palestinians amid world accusations his Jerusalem policy is hurting Middle East peace.
Israeli media predicted a marathon session that would end early on Friday with cabinet approval to implement the first of three troop redeployments in mainly rural areas of the West Bank.
"If we complete it tonight, I imagine that tomorrow we will already be able to talk with the Palestinians about our implementation process," Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh told Israel's army radio.
Israel hopes to ease Palestinian anger over a decision last week to build 6,500 homes for Jews at Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arab East Jerusalem on a tree-lined hill called Har Homa by Israel.
The cabinet session got under way three hours late, at 1800 GMT, because Netanyahu first met Jewish settler leaders angered over what one called his generosity towards the Palestinians.

Netanyahu, a right-winger elected nine months ago on a promise to get tough in talks with the Palestinians, is bound by an agreement reached in January to hand over more West Bank territory by Friday.

It was unclear how much land Israel would agree to transfer. A decision to pull back from only tiny areas could spark more friction with Palestinians already fuming over Israeli actions in East Jerusalem.

"The guiding principle is that security will not be harmed and that it will be possible to transfer a piece (of territory)...so that the peace process with the Palestinians continues," Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai told reporters.
Mordechai said that once the decision was made, it would take the army at least 48 hours to pull back.
While the cabinet met, dozens of right-wing protesters demonstrated outside the Prime Minister's office, holding signs reading: "It's not peace, it's piece by piece" and "Settlement Now".
Netanyahu also faced the wrath of Jewish settler leaders, once fervent allies who helped propel him to power.

"The prime minister has abandoned his positions and all his obligations...he has started to speak in generous terms towards the Arabs. This is grounds for divorce," Pinhas Wallerstein, head of the Council of Jewish Settlers, told reporters.
But Education Minister Zvulun Hammer said that his National Religious Party, which champions Jewish settlement, would remain in the government to try and limit the scope of future withdrawals.

On the diplomatic front, the United States, Europe and Arab states have joined Palestinians in criticising Israeli decisions over the last 10 days to build Har Homa and to close four Palestinian offices in East Jerusalem.

Israeli officials suggested the pending withdrawal -- expected in up to three areas of the West Bank including the town of Halhoul near Hebron -- might be delayed until Palestinian President Yasser Arafat shuts the PLO offices.

Israeli police gave the offices until Sunday to close willingly or be forced shut, saying they were fronts for the Palestinian self-rule Authority which cannot operate in Jerusalem under Israel-PLO peace deals.

Israel captured East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East war and annexed it, a move not recognised internationally, to claim all of the city as its capital. Palestinians regard East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state.

The sides are due to negotiate the city's fate in talks due to run until May 1999. Washington, Israel's closest ally, has joined Egypt, Britain, Germany, Russia and the European Union in criticising the actions.

Israel has handed over seven West Bank towns and most of an eighth to Palestinian self-rule since its landmark 1993 peace deal with the PLO. It has also given its former arch-foe civil responsibilities in some 450 villages.
